newsitem.title: UK: UK unit trust investors still wary of Labour - poll.
newsitem.headline: UK unit trust investors still wary of Labour - poll.

text.p: One in three UK unit trust investors still fears a Labour government, according to the latest annual survey conducted by Gavin Anderson & Company, unchanged from perceptions recorded in a poll a year ago.

Some 37 percent of consumers polled feel that a Labour election victory might harm investment propsects in the sector and a further 32 percent feel a Labour government would have no direct effect at all.
One in four felt it was impossible to say how Labour might affect the unit trust market. Seven percent felt the party might improve prospects for unit trusts.

Gavin Anderson & Company, which managed the survey of 600 unit trust and personal equity plan investors conducted between November 25 and December 13 last year, said the results were "almost identical" to the previous survey.

Account manager James White said the findings were also in keeping with the tenor of recent opinion polls, which suggest that support for the two main political parties has remained fairly constant, "despite attempts by both parties to suggest otherwise".

The survey also showed more consumers intended to buy unit trusts than a year ago, but conversely, levels of pessimism about the future of the sector had risen for the first time in recent years. The present survey is the 24th conducted.
The main reason for that pessimism is the possibility of a Labour government (26 percent) and expectations of a market correction (23 percent of respondents, from 10 percent last year).

"The vast majority of consumers (90 percent) are aware of the impact of the Morgan Grenfell/Peter Young affair. However, the majority (59 percent) of those surveyed do not consider that this has made them concerned in any way about the safety of unit trusts as an investment vehicle," the poll report said.

"The majority of those expressing some concerns about unit trusts as a result of this affair (24 percent) had "only slight' concerns." The report said the survey was conducted before top Morgan Grenfell fund manager Nicola Horlick quit the company.
